authoring: Six Mid/Low responses rewritten directly by the assistant in a conversational register. High responses are copied unchanged from the source-corrected version when saving.
scope: Historical account of the consolidated 2025 ordinance, which was replaced by the 2026 Act. Verified statutory details are retained; this is not current legal advice.

responses.DIG_01|Explicit|Mid: Say a group still has your data, but you no longer want it used. What could you do? Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025 let you take back consent and ask for deletion under Section 13. Consent means your permission. A quick date check first: the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 later replaced this ordinance. So we're talking about the old rules, not the law now in force. You'd deal with the data-fiduciary, meaning the person or group in charge of using your data. You could take back all your permission or just part. That could cover storage, other uses, or decisions made by a computer. Would that make an earlier lawful use illegal? No, taking back consent didn't undo its earlier effect. You'd put your request in writing under Section 10. The group had to check how private the data was and the risk of fraud. It had to keep an audit record and let you know what it did. There were several reasons to ask for deletion under Section 13. Perhaps the first purpose had ended, or you'd taken back the consent used for the data. Perhaps you'd objected as the ordinance allowed. Or the data had been used against the law. Deletion could also be needed to meet a law or another rule. Here's the catch: not every request meant every record had to go. Section 13 listed ID-related data while consent still applied, records kept for preservation or archives, and records kept to meet a legal duty. It also listed data classed as confidential or restricted. Those weren't reasons to brush off every request, though. And you didn't have to think only about the main file. Section 14 covered changes across linked systems too. The main group had to check the change or deletion, then tell the National Data Management Authority. That's the public body in charge. It could tell other groups and processors to make the same change. A processor uses data for the main group. Changes and replies had to go into a record that couldn't be altered, using blockchain or a similar system. That covered mirrors, caches, backups, disaster-recovery systems, test systems, and migration datasets too. Think of spare copies, recovery after a failure, testing, and data moved between systems. Rules set the time to finish those steps. But what if deleting something would distort a record? Under Section 14, only certain records approved by the Authority could be kept for that reason. These were public-interest data or archival, scientific, or historical records. The group had to say why, and you could appeal. What if it just kept using your data? Section 43 covered continued storage, use, or sharing after consent was withdrawn or lawful retention ended. It also covered failure to carry out required deletion, correction, or restriction within 30 days without undue delay. The maximum was three years in prison, BDT 500,000, or both. Don't assume that applied from day one, though. Section 1(3) delayed Sections 31-46 until a government-notified date after 18 months from issue. When writing your request, be clear about the data to delete and the consent you're taking back. If the group keeps something, ask it to explain why in writing.

responses.DIG_02|Explicit|Mid: What could an app or website do with a child's data? Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025 set out two important limits. Let's walk through them. The Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 later replaced the ordinance, so this explains the older rules, not current law. Who counted as a child? Section 2 said someone under 18, or an age set by the government. The group in charge of using data was the data-fiduciary. Under Section 9, it had to follow the set process to collect or use a child's data. It needed consent from a parent, legal guardian, or someone with power to decide for the child. Consent means freely given, informed, clear and specific permission, and the child's rights and interests had to be protected, not harmed. Was it enough for someone just to say, 'I'm the parent'? No. Section 38 required consent that came first and could be checked. The group had to take reasonable steps to check the guardian's identity and right to give consent. Here's the other limit. Section 9 banned using a particular child's behavior or other data for tracking, monitoring, profiling, or targeted ads. Tracking or monitoring means following or watching what the child does. Profiling means using data to infer their interests or habits. Targeted ads are picked for someone using their data. Could a parent's permission remove that ban? No, the two rules were separate. But this wasn't a ban on every ad or every use of a child's data. How long did consent last? Section 9 said until the child turned 18. For someone who couldn't give consent, it lasted until that person gained the ability to do so. What if a group broke the consent rules? Section 38 covered collecting, processing, or using a child's data without the required prior consent. It also covered failing to take reasonable steps to check the guardian's identity and authority. The maximum was three years in prison, BDT 500,000, or both. That's a maximum, not a fixed sentence for every case. There's a timing point too. Section 1(3) delayed Sections 31-46 until a government-notified date after 18 months from issue. So the penalty rules didn't all start on the day the ordinance was issued. The key thing to remember is this: getting proper consent and avoiding the banned uses were two separate duties. A group had to meet both, not just ask a parent to say yes.

responses.DIG_03|Explicit|Mid: What if someone takes or shares your data without being allowed to? The answer depends on what they did and why. Let's look at Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025. The Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 later replaced it, so we're discussing the older rules, not current law. Personal data can identify you. Think of bank details, location data, or biometric data such as fingerprints. Processing doesn't just mean collecting it. It includes storing, using, sharing, and transferring it too. Was every use without consent a crime? No. Consent means permission, but another legal basis could also allow a use. That's why the details matter. Section 36 covered processing data without the required consent or legal basis. It also covered giving, transferring, or showing data to another party, or receiving it from them. The person had to act with dishonest intent or an aim to benefit. The maximum was five years in prison, BDT 1,000,000, or both. That wasn't a fixed penalty for every mistake. What about especially private data? Section 37 covered sensitive data used in breach of Section 7 or another rule. It applied where there was no explicit consent or another legal basis. Sensitive data includes health records, religious beliefs, and fingerprints. Explicit consent means clear permission. The maximum was seven years in prison, BDT 2,000,000, or both. What if someone got into a system and took data? Section 39 covered taking or intercepting data without authority after gaining access. That could be access to a system, device, or database. It also covered intercepting messages or data flows while personal data was being sent. Intercepting means catching data as it passes between places. The maximum was five years in prison, BDT 1,000,000, or both. Could someone get consent by tricking you? Section 40 covered ways of getting consent unfairly. These included deception, force, a false identity, false statements, or other unfair means. It also covered collecting or using data through that consent. Knowingly receiving such data for profit or an unfair purpose was covered too. The maximum was five years in prison, BDT 1,000,000, or both. What if someone got data through their job? Section 41 covered sharing, transferring, or using sensitive or identifying data gained through official or contract work. It also covered using or processing data for a purpose the ordinance didn't allow. It applied to data-fiduciaries, who control data use, and processors, who use data for them. Staff, contractors, and agents were covered too. The maximum was five years in prison, BDT 1,500,000, or both. Could someone get a penalty just for helping? Section 44 gave the same penalty to a person or group that supported, approved, or helped an offence. Who would hear the case? Under Section 45, the Cyber Tribunal would try these cases. That's the court named for these trials. And no, the ordinance didn't set a death penalty for these offences. Sections 54 and 55 dealt with emergency orders and an official English text, not the penalty rules. One last point: these were maximum penalties, not automatic sentences. Under Section 1(3), Sections 31-46 needed an official start date. The government had to name that date after 18 months from issue. They didn't all start on the day the ordinance was issued. So a group had to check its consent or legal basis, get genuine consent where needed, and keep access, use, and sharing within what was allowed.

responses.DIG_01|Explicit|High: Under Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025, withdrawal of consent and erasure are governed principally by Section 13, rather than Section 23. This is a historical account of the ordinance: the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 subsequently repealed it. The provisions described here should not be assumed to establish the law currently in force. A data-fiduciary is the person or organization responsible for processing personal data. Section 13 allows the data subject to withdraw consent wholly or partly for storage, processing, or automated decisions. Withdrawal does not retrospectively invalidate processing undertaken while consent remained effective. Under Section 10, rights are exercised through a written application to the data-fiduciary. The organization must consider the sensitivity of the data and the risk of fraud, retain an audit record of its actions, and inform the applicant. Section 13 identifies grounds for erasure, including the original purpose no longer existing, withdrawal of the consent on which processing depended, an objection made under the ordinance, unlawful processing, or deletion needed to meet a legal obligation or prescribed condition. The right is qualified. Section 13 also lists possible grounds for refusing deletion: identification-related data while consent continues, preservation or archival purposes, legal retention duties, and data classified as confidential or restricted. These are statutory categories, not permission to refuse every request. Section 14 provides for system-wide propagation of approved changes. The primary data-fiduciary verifies the deletion or update and notifies the National Data Management Authority. The Authority directs relevant secondary data-fiduciaries and processors to implement the approved change and records the changes and acknowledgments in an immutable ledger, using blockchain or equivalent technology. The process extends to copies in mirrors, caches, backups, disaster-recovery systems, test environments, and migration datasets. Regulations determine implementation timelines. Where erasure would distort a record, Section 14 permits refusal only for Authority-designated public-interest data or archival, scientific, or historical records. The refusal must give reasons and can be appealed. Section 43 prescribes an offence for continued storage, use, or disclosure after consent withdrawal or expiry of lawful retention, or failure to implement the required erasure, correction, or restriction without undue delay within 30 days of a request. Its maximum penalty is three years' imprisonment, BDT 500,000, or both. However, Section 1(3) deferred commencement of Sections 31-46 until a government-notified date after 18 months from issuance. The prescribed penalty therefore must not be presented as automatically enforceable from the ordinance's publication date. For an erasure request, identify the relevant records, specify any consent being withdrawn, and ask for a written explanation of any retention ground or refusal.
responses.DIG_02|Explicit|High: Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025 provided child-specific safeguards in Section 9. This account concerns the ordinance, which was later repealed by the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026; it should not be treated as a statement of current law. Section 2 defined a child as a person under 18 or an age specified by the government. Under Section 9, a data-fiduciary could collect or process a child's personal data through the prescribed procedure with consent from a parent, legal guardian, or person empowered to decide on the child's behalf. A data-fiduciary is the person or organization responsible for processing the data. Processing had to protect the child's rights and interests, rather than undermine them. Section 38 required prior verifiable parental or legal-guardian consent and reasonable steps to establish the consenting guardian's identity and authority. Consent therefore involved more than an unchecked assertion that someone was a parent. Section 9 prohibited using a particular child's behavior or other data for tracking, monitoring, profiling, or targeted advertising. Profiling means evaluating personal information to infer characteristics such as interests, habits, or behavior. This prohibition was distinct from the consent requirement: obtaining a parent's consent did not remove the child-specific restriction. The provision should not be restated as a ban on every advertisement or every processing activity involving a child. Section 9 also stated that the relevant consent remained valid until the child reached 18. For a person unable to consent, the corresponding consent lasted until that person gained the ability to consent. Section 38 prescribed a maximum of three years' imprisonment, BDT 500,000, or both for collecting, processing, or using a child's data without the required prior verifiable consent, or failing to take reasonable steps to verify the guardian's identity and authority. Section 1(3), however, delayed commencement of Sections 31-46 until a government-notified date after 18 months from issuance. The existence of a prescribed penalty must therefore be distinguished from its immediate enforceability. The central distinction is between collecting data through a lawful consent process and using a child's behavior or data for prohibited tracking or advertising. Organizations had to address both duties; parental consent alone did not satisfy them all.
responses.DIG_03|Explicit|High: Unauthorized collection and disclosure were addressed by several distinct offences in Bangladesh's Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025. This is an account of that ordinance, not current law: the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 later repealed it. Personal data includes information that identifies a person or makes them identifiable, including financial, location, and biometric information. Processing is broader than collection: it includes storage, use, transfer, and disclosure. Absence of consent does not alone establish that every use is unlawful, because a relevant legal basis may also authorize processing. Section 36 addressed processing personal data, supplying, transferring, or disclosing it to a third party, or receiving it from a third party without the required consent or legal basis, with dishonest intent or an intention to benefit. Its maximum penalty was five years' imprisonment, BDT 1,000,000, or both. The intent requirement matters; this provision should not be described as imposing the same penalty on every accidental mistake. Section 37 addressed processing sensitive personal data in breach of Section 7 or another provision without explicit consent or another legal basis. Its maximum was seven years' imprisonment, BDT 2,000,000, or both. Sensitive data includes health information, religious beliefs, and biometric information. Section 39 covered unauthorized interception or extraction of personal data after gaining access to a system, device, or database, and interception of communications or data flows while personal data was being transmitted. Its maximum was five years' imprisonment, BDT 1,000,000, or both. Section 40 addressed obtaining consent by deception, force, impersonation, misrepresentation, or other unfair means; collecting or processing data on that basis; and knowingly receiving that data for a profitable or unfair purpose. Its maximum was five years' imprisonment, BDT 1,000,000, or both. Section 41 addressed disclosure, transfer, or use of sensitive or personally identifiable data obtained during official or contractual duties, and use or processing for a purpose not authorized under the ordinance. It covered data-fiduciaries, processors, employees, contractors, and agents. Its maximum was five years' imprisonment, BDT 1,500,000, or both. Section 44 provided the same penalty as the underlying offence for a person or institution supporting, authorizing, or assisting its commission. Section 45 assigned trials of offences under the ordinance to the Cyber Tribunal. The ordinance did not prescribe a death penalty for these offences. Sections 54 and 55 concerned emergency orders and publication of an authoritative English text, not the prison and fine provisions. Section 1(3) deferred commencement of Sections 31-46 until a government-notified date after 18 months from issuance. The listed penalties are prescribed maxima, not automatic sentences or proof that those provisions were enforceable immediately on publication. Compliance therefore required a valid consent or legal basis, genuine consent where required, access limited to authorized uses, and care when receiving or sharing another person's data.
